essays.stem: Describe the steps to set up a mail merge that makes a birthday offer letter for each client on the salon's client list.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the client list, which is the data source. It should be a table or spreadsheet with one heading row, such as First name, Last name, Address and Birth month, and one row for each client, with no blank rows. I save it with a clear name. Next I write the letter in the word processor, leaving out the parts that change for each client. I start the mail merge, choose letters, and connect the letter to the client list. I insert merge fields, such as First name and Address, where each client's details should go, and make sure there are spaces and punctuation around them. I can filter the list so that only clients with a birthday in the coming month get a letter. Then I preview the results, checking a few letters to make sure the names, addresses and layout are right. Finally I complete the merge to print the letters or to make a new document, and save it.
markingPoints: Prepares a clean data source with one heading row and one row per client
Writes the main letter and connects it to the data source
Inserts the merge fields in the right places
Filters or sorts the list where needed, for example by birth month
Previews and checks, then completes the merge to print or to a new file, and saves

essays.stem: Explain how heading styles, headers and footers, and page numbers make a long document, such as a staff handbook, easier to make and to use.
essays.modelAnswer: Heading styles give every heading of the same level the same font, size and spacing. If the salon decides to change the look, I change the style once and every heading changes, so the handbook stays neat and matching. Styles also let the program build a table of contents and a navigation pane, so staff can jump straight to a section such as 'Waxing hygiene'. A header or footer holds text that appears on every page, such as the salon's name, the title of the handbook and the date of the latest version, so a loose printed page can be identified. Page numbers are put into the header or footer as a field, so they update by themselves when pages are added or removed, and staff can find pages from the contents list. Together these features save time when writing, and make the document easier to read, update and print.
markingPoints: Styles keep headings consistent and can be changed in one place
Styles allow an automatic table of contents and quick navigation
Headers and footers repeat details such as the title and version on every page
Automatic page numbers update when pages change
Overall, they save time and make the document easier to use and update

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a relative and an absolute cell reference, using a therapist's commission sheet as an example.
essays.modelAnswer: A relative cell reference, such as B2, changes when the formula is copied to another cell. If C2 holds =B2*0.1 and I copy it down to C3, it becomes =B3*0.1. That is what I want, because each row has a different therapist's sales. An absolute cell reference, such as $E$1, has a dollar sign in front of the column letter and the row number, so it does not change when the formula is copied. In a commission sheet, the rate, for example 10%, is typed once in E1. The formula in C2 is =B2*$E$1. When I copy it down, B2 changes to B3, B4 and so on, but $E$1 stays the same, so every row uses the one rate cell. If I used =B2*E1 instead, the copied formula would become =B3*E2, which points at an empty cell and gives a wrong answer of zero. With the absolute reference, if the rate changes I change only E1.
markingPoints: A relative reference changes when the formula is copied
An absolute reference uses $ signs and does not change
Gives a commission formula such as =B2*$E$1
Explains what goes wrong if the rate cell is relative
The rate can be changed in one cell

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up a simple stock sheet in a spreadsheet that shows when each product needs to be reordered.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start a new spreadsheet and type headings in row 1: Product, Size, Stock in hand, Reorder level, Unit cost (J$), Stock value (J$) and Action. I would make the headings bold and freeze the top row so that they stay in view. I would type one product on each row, such as cleanser, toner, wax and cotton wool. In the Stock value column I would write a formula that multiplies the stock in hand by the unit cost, for example =C2*E2, and copy it down with the fill handle. In the Action column I would use an IF formula that compares the stock in hand with the reorder level and shows 'Reorder' when the stock is at or below that level, and 'OK' when it is not. I would add conditional formatting to turn the 'Reorder' cells red so they stand out. I would use SUM to total the stock value, format money as currency, and sort or filter the list to see what to reorder. Finally I would save it with a clear name and update it after each stock count.
markingPoints: Clear headings, one product per row, and the top row frozen
A stock value formula copied down with the fill handle
An IF formula comparing the stock with the reorder level
Conditional formatting to highlight items to reorder
Totals, currency format, sort or filter, and saved with a clear name

essays.stem: Describe how to make a clear chart from a spreadsheet of monthly treatment sales, and how to check it before you use it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the data: one column for the months and one for the sales in J$, with clear headings and no blank rows. I select the headings and the data, then insert a chart. For sales over a year, a line chart or a column chart works well, because it shows how sales go up and down from month to month. I add a clear chart title, such as 'Treatment sales by month, 2026 (J$)', and label the axes, with the months along the bottom and J$ up the side. With only one set of figures I can remove the legend, but I keep it if I compare two years. I choose plain, readable colours and make the text large enough. Before I use the chart, I check that every month is shown in the right order, that the figures match the table, that the scale makes sense and that nothing is cut off. Then I place it in the report or on a slide and save the file.
markingPoints: Checks and selects clean data with headings
Chooses a suitable chart type and says why
Adds a clear title and axis labels, and a legend where needed
Uses plain, readable formatting
Checks the chart against the data before using it

essays.stem: Explain what makes a good slide presentation for training new staff on a spa's services.
essays.modelAnswer: A good training presentation is planned around what new staff need to know, such as the list of services, how long each one takes, the price in J$ and the main safety points. It starts with a title slide and an outline, then has one main idea on each slide, with short points rather than long paragraphs. The text is large, with dark text on a plain light background, so it can be read from the back of the room. The same design, fonts and colours are used on every slide, ideally set up once with the slide master, so it looks professional. Clear photos or simple diagrams help, for example a picture of a set-up trolley. Transitions and animations are used only a little, so they do not distract. The presenter puts extra details in the speaker notes, checks the spelling, and runs through the slide show before the session. Handouts can be printed so that staff can take notes.
markingPoints: Planned around what new staff need, with a title slide and an outline
One idea per slide, with short points
Large, high-contrast text and the same design on every slide
Helpful pictures and few distracting effects
Uses speaker notes, checks spelling, rehearses, and gives handouts

essays.stem: Explain how a salon should protect client information kept on its computers and phones.
essays.modelAnswer: Client records hold private details such as names, phone numbers, addresses, allergies and medical notes, so they must be kept safe and used only for the salon's work. Each member of staff should have their own login, with a strong password that is not shared or written down near the computer. Files with client details should be kept in a protected folder that only the staff who need them can open. Screens should be locked when staff leave the desk, and placed so that clients cannot read them. Antivirus software and updates should be kept up to date. Staff should not send client details to their own phones or post anything about clients on social media. Emails should be checked so that they go to the right person, and group emails should use 'bcc' so that addresses are not shown to everyone. Backups should be kept somewhere secure, old records deleted or shredded when the policy says, and any loss of data reported to the manager at once.
markingPoints: Client data is private and used only for the salon's work
Own logins and strong passwords, and locked screens
Protected folders that only those who need them can open
No client details on personal phones or social media; emails checked, and bcc for groups
Antivirus and updates, secure backups, safe disposal, and reporting any loss

essays.stem: Describe a good system for naming, filing and backing up the salon's computer files.
essays.modelAnswer: The salon should agree one folder structure that everyone uses, for example main folders for Clients, Stock, Staff rotas, Price lists and Marketing, with sub-folders for each year or month. File names should be clear and follow the same pattern, such as what the file is, then the date written year-month-day, for example 'Stock count 2026-07-31'. This way files sort in date order and anyone can find them. Staff should avoid names like 'New document' or 'Final final'. Old versions can be moved to an Archive folder instead of being mixed with the current ones. Files should be saved often while working. Backups should be made regularly, for example at the end of each day or week, onto a separate drive or secure online storage, and one copy should be kept away from the salon in case of fire or theft. Someone should check from time to time that the backup can really be opened. Private client files are kept in protected folders.
markingPoints: An agreed folder structure that everyone uses
Clear file names with the date in a set pattern
Old versions archived, and files saved often
Regular backups to a separate drive or secure online storage, with a copy kept away from the salon
Checks that backups open, and protects private files

essays.stem: Explain how to share a document online with co-workers safely, and how comments and version history help the team.
essays.modelAnswer: I save the document in the salon's shared online storage, not in a personal account. I share it only with the co-workers who need it, using their work email addresses, and I choose the right permission for each person: 'view' for those who only need to read it, 'comment' for those who should suggest changes, and 'edit' only for those who must change it. I do not make the link open to anyone, especially if the file has client or staff details. Comments let co-workers ask questions or suggest changes beside the text without changing it, and the person in charge can reply and mark each one as done. Version history keeps a record of earlier copies and shows who changed what and when. If someone deletes or changes something by mistake, an earlier version can be restored. This means the team works on one up-to-date copy instead of emailing many different versions to each other.
markingPoints: Saves in the salon's shared storage and shares only with those who need it
Chooses the right permission: view, comment or edit
Does not make links open to anyone for private files
Comments allow suggestions and questions without changing the text
Version history shows changes and lets earlier copies be restored

essays.stem: Describe how to design a one-page promotional flyer for a spa offer in a word processor, using pictures, text wrapping, and columns or a table.
essays.modelAnswer: First I plan the flyer: the offer, the price in J$, the dates and the contact details. I set the page size and margins, and choose portrait or landscape. I type a short, bold heading at the top, such as 'Mother's Day Pamper Package', using a heading style so that it is large and clear. I insert a photo of the spa or a treatment and set the text wrapping, for example square or top and bottom, so the text flows neatly around it. I resize the photo from a corner so that it does not stretch. For the list of treatments and prices I use a table or two columns, so that everything lines up. I keep to two or three fonts and colours that match the spa's look, with dark text on a light background. I put the contact details and any conditions in the footer. Then I check the spelling and prices, look at it in print preview, print one test copy, and save it, also as a PDF for sending.
markingPoints: Plans the content and sets up the page
A clear heading using a style
Inserts a picture, sets the text wrapping and resizes it in proportion
Uses a table or columns for treatments and prices, with few fonts and colours
Checks spelling, prices and print preview, then saves, also as a PDF

practical1.title: Mail-merged birthday offer letters from a client list
practical1.brief: Use the Centre's computer to make personal birthday offer letters for a spa's clients. Use only the made-up client details on the assessor's card, never real client details. Share the stages so that each member works at the computer for at least one stage while the others watch and check: (1) make a group folder and, in a spreadsheet, type the client list with the headings First name, Last name, Address line 1, Town, Birth month and Favourite treatment (at least 10 clients), then save it with a clear name, (2) in the word processor, write the letter: the spa's name and logo in the header, a heading style for the title, a short table of three birthday offers with prices in J$, and the spa's phone number and the page number in the footer, (3) start the mail merge, connect the letter to the client list, and insert the merge fields for the name, address and favourite treatment, (4) filter the list so that only clients with a birthday in the month the assessor names are included, and preview at least three letters, (5) complete the merge to a new document, save it, and save one letter as a PDF. In a group of 4, one member does two stages. Each member then explains one feature to the assessor. Take a photo of the screen (or a screenshot) at each stage below and add them to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A computer with word-processing and spreadsheet programs, and a printer
A card with made-up client details (at least 10 clients), and the spa's logo file
The birthday offers and their prices in J$, from the assessor
The Centre's shared folder or a USB flash drive
A phone or camera to photograph the screen
photos: The group folder and the saved client list with its headings
The letter with the header, heading style, offers table and footer showing
The merge fields inserted in the letter
The filter set on the birth month
The preview of a merged letter showing one client's details
The finished merged document and the PDF in the group folder
checklist: Typed the client list accurately, with one heading row and no blank rows
Used a heading style, a table, and a header and footer correctly
Connected the letter to the client list and inserted the right merge fields
Filtered the list correctly and previewed the letters
Completed the merge, saved with clear file names and made a PDF
Explained one feature clearly to the assessor
Used only made-up client details and left the computer logged off and tidy
safety: Sit with your back supported, feet flat and the screen at eye level
Take short breaks from the screen, and look away into the distance every so often
Keep drinks away from the computer and keep cables out of walkways
Use only made-up client details; never copy real client records

practical2.title: Weekly takings and commission spreadsheet, with a chart for a staff meeting
practical2.brief: Use the Centre's computer to build a spreadsheet of one week's takings for a salon and spa, from the assessor's data card: five made-up therapists, their takings in J$ for each day from Monday to Saturday, a weekly target and a commission rate. Share the stages so that each member works at the computer for at least one stage while the others watch and check: (1) set up the headings, type in the data, and format the money as J$, (2) use SUM for each therapist's weekly total and each day's total, and AVERAGE and MAX for the week, (3) type the commission rate in its own labelled cell and work out each therapist's commission with a formula that uses an absolute reference, then copy it down, (4) use an IF formula to show 'Target met' or 'Not yet', add conditional formatting to highlight 'Target met', and sort the therapists by weekly total, (5) make a column chart of the weekly totals with a title and axis labels, put it on a slide in a three-slide presentation (title, chart, two key points), and print it as a handout. In a group of 4, one member does two stages. Each member then explains one formula or feature to the assessor. Take a photo of the screen (or a screenshot) at each stage below and add them to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A computer with spreadsheet and presentation programs, and a printer
A data card from the assessor: daily takings in J$ for five made-up therapists, a weekly target and a commission rate
The Centre's shared folder or a USB flash drive
A phone or camera to photograph the screen
photos: The headings and data typed in, with money shown as J$
The SUM, AVERAGE and MAX formulas shown in the formula bar
The commission formula with the absolute reference in the formula bar, filled down
The IF results with the conditional formatting, and the list sorted
The finished column chart with its title and axis labels
The chart on the slide, and the printed handout next to the screen
checklist: Typed the data accurately and formatted money as J$
Used SUM, AVERAGE and MAX correctly
Used an absolute reference for the commission rate and copied the formula correctly
Wrote a correct IF formula and set the conditional formatting
Sorted the data without mixing up the rows
Made a clear, correctly labelled chart and placed it on a slide
Checked at least two results with a calculator and explained one formula to the assessor
safety: Sit with good posture, the screen at eye level and the wrists straight
Take short breaks from the screen, and look away into the distance every so often
Keep drinks away from the computer and keep cables out of walkways
Report any damaged cable or plug and do not use it
